1
藝文一《易》曰：“觀乎天文，以察時變； 觀乎人文，以化成天下。” 文之有關於世運，尚矣。 然書契以來，文字多而世代日降； 秦火而後，文字多而世教日興，其故何哉？ 蓋世道升降，人心習俗之致然，非徒文字之所為也。 然去古既遠，苟無斯文以範防之，則愈趨而愈下矣。 故由秦而降，每以斯文之盛衰，占斯世之治忽焉。 宋有天下，先後三百餘年，考其治化之汙隆，風氣之離合，雖不足以擬倫三代，然其時君汲汲於道藝，輔治之臣莫不以經術為先務，學士搢紳先生，談道德性命之學，不絕於口，豈不彬彬乎進於周之文哉！ 宋之不競，或以為文勝之弊，遂歸咎焉，此以功利為言，未必知道者之論也。 曆代之書籍，莫厄於秦，莫富於隋、唐。 隋嘉則殿書三十七萬卷。 而唐之藏書，開元最盛，為卷八萬有奇。 其間唐人所自為書，幾三萬卷，則舊書之傳者，至是蓋亦鮮矣。 陵遲逮於五季，幹戈相尋，海寓鼎沸，斯民不復見《詩》、《書》、《禮》、《樂》之化。 周顯德中，始有經籍刻板，學者無筆劄之勞，獲睹古人全書。 然亂離以來，編帙散佚，幸而存者，百無二三。 宋初，有書萬餘卷。 其後削平諸國，收其圖籍，及下詔遣使購求散亡，三館之書，稍復增益。 太宗始於左升龍門北建崇文院，而徙三館之書以實之。 又分三館書萬餘卷，別為書庫，目曰“秘閣”。 閣成，親臨幸觀書，賜從臣及直館宴。 又命近習侍衛之臣縱觀群書。 真宗時，命三館寫四部書二本，置禁中之龍圖閣及後苑之太清樓，而玉宸殿、四門殿亦各有書萬餘卷。 又以秘閣地隘，分內藏西庫以廣之，其右文之意，亦雲至矣。 已而王宮火，延及崇文、秘閣，書多煨燼。 其僅存者，遷於右掖門外，謂之崇文外院，命重寫書籍，選官詳覆校勘，常以參知政事一人領之，書成，歸於太清樓。 仁宗既新作崇文院，命翰林學士張觀等編四庫書，仿《開元四部録》為《崇文總目》，書凡三萬六百六十九卷。 神宗改官制，遂廢館職，以崇文院為秘書省，秘閣經籍圖書以秘書郎主之，編輯校定，正其脫誤，則主於校書郎。 徽宗時，更《崇文總目》之號為《秘書總目》。 詔購求士民藏書，其有所秘未見之書足備觀采者，仍命以官。 且以三館書多逸遺，命建局以補全校正為名，設官總理，募工繕寫。 一置宣和殿，一置太清樓，一置秘閣。 自熙寧以來，搜訪補輯，至是為盛矣。 嚐曆考之，始太祖、太宗、真宗三朝，三千三百二十七部，三萬九千一百四十二卷。 次仁、英兩朝，一千四百七十二部，八千四百四十六卷。 次神、哲、徽、欽四朝，一千九百六部，二萬六千二百八十九卷。 三朝所録，則兩朝不復登載，而録其所未有者。 四朝於兩朝亦然。 最其當時之目，為部六千七百有五，為卷七萬三千八百七十有七焉。 迨夫靖康之難，而宣和、館閣之儲蕩然靡遺。 高宗移蹕臨安，乃建秘書省於國史院之右，搜訪遺闕，屢優獻書之賞，於是四方之藏，稍稍復出，而館閣編輯，日益以富矣。 當時類次書目，得四萬四千四百八十六卷。 至寧宗時續書目，又得一萬四千九百四十三卷，視《崇文總目》，又有加焉。 自是而後，迄於終祚，國步艱難，軍旅之事，日不暇給，而君臣上下，未嚐頃刻不以文學為務，大而朝廷，微而草野，其所製作、講說、紀述、賦詠，動成卷帙，累而數之，有非前代之所及也。 雖其間釽裂大道，疣贅聖謨，幽怪恍惚，瑣碎支離有所不免，然而瑕瑜相形，雅鄭各趣，譬之萬派歸海，四瀆可分，繁星麗天，五緯可識，求約於博，則有要存焉。 宋舊史，自太祖至寧宗，為書凡四。 誌藝文者，前後部帙，有亡增損，互有異同。 今刪其重復，合為一誌，蓋以寧宗以後史之所未録者，仿前史分經、史、子、集四類而條列之，大凡為書九千八百十九部，十一萬九千九百七十二卷雲。 經類十：一曰《易》類，二曰《書》類，三曰《詩》類，四曰《禮》類，五曰《樂》類，六曰《春秋》類，七曰《孝經》類，八曰《論語》類，九曰經解類，十曰小學類。
Arts and Literature 1. The Book of Changes says: "Look to the patterns of heaven to read the turning of the seasons; observe the patterns of human affairs to civilize and perfect the realm." That writing and culture matter to the rise and fall of an age has been clear for a very long time. Yet from the time writing was invented, although texts grew ever more numerous, each generation seemed to decline further; yet after the Qin bibliocaust, although texts again multiplied, moral instruction in the world rose day by day—what is the reason? It is surely because the ascent or descent of the age and the drift of popular hearts and customs bring this about—not writing by itself. But once antiquity lies far behind, unless this literary culture is used as a barrier and safeguard, society only slides further down. Hence from the Qin dynasty onward, each age has been read by whether literary culture waxed or waned—by that sign one judged order or disorder. The Song held the empire for over three centuries; weighing the ebb and flow of its rule and the unity or fracture of its mores, it may not equal the Three Dynasties, yet its emperors pressed hard after the Way and the arts, every minister who aided rule put the classics first, and literati, officials, and masters never ceased discussing the philosophy of nature and principle—was this not a cultured advance toward the brilliance of Zhou! Some say the Song lost its edge because culture grew too strong and blame literature for it—but that is the language of profit and utility, not necessarily the judgment of one who understands the Way. Books of successive dynasties met no disaster like the Qin burning, and no hoard like those of Sui and Tang. Sui's Hall of Accumulated Virtue held 370,000 juan. Tang imperial collections peaked under Kaiyuan at a little over 80,000 juan. Nearly 30,000 juan were works Tang authors wrote themselves, so of older texts still handed down, few indeed survived by then. Decay ran on into the Five Dynasties: war followed war, the empire boiled, and the people no longer knew the civilizing power of the Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music. Under Later Zhou's Xiande reign, classics were first cut on blocks; scholars no longer had to copy by hand and could read whole ancient books. But since the chaos, codices had scattered and vanished; of what still existed, scarcely two or three in a hundred. Early in the Song there were a little over ten thousand juan. Later, when the rival states were subdued, their maps and libraries were taken in; edicts sent envoys to buy up what had been lost, and the Three Institutes' holdings slowly grew again. Taizong first built the Chongwen Court north of the Left Ascending Dragon Gate and moved the Three Institutes' books there to stock it. He also set aside more than ten thousand juan from the Three Institutes into a separate library called the Secret Repository. When it was finished, he visited in person to read, and feasted his ministers and institute staff. He also commanded personal attendants and guards to roam freely among the collections. Under Zhenzong the Three Institutes copied the four categories in two sets each, one for the Dragon Diagram Pavilion in the palace and one for the Great Clarity Tower in the rear garden; the Jade Hall and Four Gates Hall each held over ten thousand juan as well. The Secret Repository grounds were cramped, so part of the inner treasury's west store was opened to expand it—his esteem for letters could hardly go further. Soon a fire in the royal palace reached the Chongwen Court and Secret Repository, and many books were burned to ash. What little remained was moved outside the Right Arm Gate as the Outer Chongwen Court; he ordered books recopied and officials chosen for careful collation, usually led by one Vice Grand Councillor; finished copies went back to the Great Clarity Tower. Renzong rebuilt the Chongwen Court and had Hanlin academician Zhang Guan and others compile the four repositories, following the Kaiyuan Four-Category Catalogue to produce the Comprehensive Catalogue of the Chongwen Court—30,669 juan in all. Shenzong reformed offices, abolished institute posts, made the Chongwen Court the Secretariat, put Secretariat Gentlemen over the Secret Repository's classics and maps, and Collators over editing, collation, and correction of errors. Under Huizong the Comprehensive Catalogue of the Chongwen Court was renamed the Comprehensive Secretariat Catalogue. An edict purchased books from private collections; owners of rare unseen works fit for the court still received official appointment. Many Three Institutes books were lost, so he set up a bureau for full supplementation and collation, with supervising officials and hired copyists. One copy went to the Xuanhe Hall, one to the Great Clarity Tower, one to the Secret Repository. Since Xining, search and repair had continued; by then the collection was at its fullest. Reviewing the registers: first the three reigns of Taizu, Taizong, and Zhenzong—3,327 titles in 39,142 juan. Next Renzong and Yingzong—1,472 titles, 8,446 juan. Next Shenzong, Zhezong, Huizong, and Qinzong—1,906 titles, 26,289 juan. What the three earlier reigns listed was not repeated for the two later ones; only new acquisitions were entered. The four-reign register did the same with the two-reign one. At the peak count of that era there were 6,705 titles and 73,877 juan. Then came the disaster of Jingkang, and the Xuanhe and institute holdings were utterly lost. Gaozong moved the court to Lin'an, built the Secretariat east of the National History Institute, sought lost works, repeatedly rewarded book donors, and collections from all quarters slowly returned while institute holdings grew richer by the day. The classified catalogue of that time reached 44,486 juan. Ningzong's continuation added another 14,943 juan—beyond the Comprehensive Catalogue of the Chongwen Court. From then until the dynasty fell, though the realm was hard pressed and war consumed every day, court and countryside never ceased literary work; compositions, lectures, chronicles, and poems piled into volumes—taken together, beyond any earlier age. To be sure, the corpus also holds ruptures of the great Way, excrescences on sage teaching, occult vagueness, and petty fragments—yet flaw and gem lie side by side, elegant and vulgar each keep their place; like myriad streams to the sea or stars in the sky, from abundance one can still find the essential. The old Song histories from Taizu to Ningzong were four separate works. Their arts-and-letters treatises, fascicle by fascicle, differed in omissions, additions, and wording. Duplicates are now removed and merged into one treatise; works after Ningzong that earlier histories omitted are listed under classics, histories, masters, and collections as before—in all 9,819 titles and 119,972 juan. Classics fall into ten types: Changes, Documents, Odes, Rites, Music, Spring and Autumn, Filial Piety, Analects, exegetical works, and philology.
